outcome: Still open as of 11 October 2026. Since 26 January 2024: a bounded computer search (Grantham, arXiv 2024) found no Goormaghtigh prime below 10⁷⁰⁰ beyond 31 and 8191; a 2025 paper restates the conjecture and proves only a conditional implication about a different object; a 2025 paper on a related fixed-N equation does not touch the full equation; and a self-published, unrefereed Hugging Face manuscript from 28 September 2026 claims a reduction to abc-type triples, and its own proof-boundary file says the conjecture is not proved. No source names an AI system as involved in any of this.
problem_asks: (a) Determine every integer solution (x, y, m, n) of (xᵐ − 1)/(x − 1) = (yⁿ − 1)/(y − 1) with x > y > 1 and m, n > 2, in the statement's ordering. Bennett et al. and Grantham write the larger base as y, so the letters swap between sources. (b) The conjecture, as the literature states it, asserts there are exactly two solutions: (x, y, m, n) = (5, 2, 3, 5) and (90, 2, 3, 13), giving the common values N = 31 = 11111₂ = 111₅ and N = 8191 = 1111111111111₂ = 111₉₀. The statement as given does not spell out this answer; it is supplied by the cited conjecture. (c) Implicit in (a) and (b): whether the equation has finitely many solutions at all. The conjecture entails this; it is unknown unconditionally. (d) Equivalent form used in the literature: numbers that are repunits with at least three digits in two different bases. The case m = 2 is excluded by the statement.

events.what_happened: Davenport, Lewis and Schinzel (1961): for fixed exponents m and n, the equation has only finitely many solutions. The proof is ineffective (relies on Siegel's theorem). Reported in the Wikipedia article as summarised by the fetch tool; the 1961 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Finiteness of solutions (x, y) when the exponent pair (m, n) is fixed. Restriction: exponents fixed in advance, bounds ineffective; says nothing about x, y, m, n jointly.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: no bound on m, n jointly; finiteness unknown unconditionally for the full equation.
events.direction: Partial finiteness result; consistent with the conjecture, proves no classification.

events.what_happened: Bateman and Stemmler, Illinois J. Math. 6 (1962), using computations by Horn: the only N below about 1.275 × 10¹⁰ with two repunit representations in which x, y and N are all prime is N = 31. Taken from Grantham's reference list and introduction, both opened; the 1962 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Classification restricted to prime N, prime x and prime y, below 1.275 × 10¹⁰: only 31. Restriction: all three of N, x, y prime, and the size bound.
events.remains: The non-prime cases; prime cases above 1.275 × 10¹⁰ (later extended by Grantham 2024 to N prime below 10⁷⁰⁰, without the prime-base restriction recorded here); the full classification.
events.directly_checkable: A finite computation; method not reviewed here.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the restricted prime case; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Balasubramanian and Shorey (1980): finitely many solutions when the prime divisors of x and y lie in a given finite set, with the solutions effectively computable. Per the Wikipedia article as summarised by the fetch tool; the 1980 paper was not opened.

events.remains: Bases with unbounded prime divisors; the exponents jointly; the full classification.
events.direction: Partial result, consistent with the conjecture; no classification.

events.what_happened: Nesterenko and Shorey (1998), 'On the equation of Goormaghtigh': under the exponent structure m − 1 = dr, n − 1 = ds with d > 1, max(x, y, m, n) is bounded by a computable constant depending on r and s. Per the Wikipedia article as summarised; the 1998 paper was not opened.

events.remains: Exponent pairs without that shared-factor structure, including the case gcd(m−1, n−1) = 1 in general; the full classification.
events.direction: Partial effective finiteness; consistent with the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Jon Grantham, 'No new Goormaghtigh primes up to 10⁷⁰⁰', arXiv:2410.03677 (v1 posted 19 Sep 2024), published in Integers 24 (2024), paper A98, 4 pp. Searches for prime N with two repunit representations (xᵐ − 1)/(x − 1) = (yⁿ − 1)/(y − 1) with at least three digits and finds no others below 10⁷⁰⁰. Method: a residue sieve over odd prime exponents m (m ≥ 53 in this range) and n, using the Bennett–Garbuz–Martens Theorem 6 and the Bennett–Gherga–Kreso restriction to exclude a case; about 480 core-days on a single core. Also proves conditionally, assuming the abc conjecture (argument credited to a suggestion by Carl Pomerance), that there are finitely many Goormaghtigh numbers where neither representation has length 3 or 4 (Theorem 2), and hence finitely many Goormaghtigh primes (Corollary 1, with Bennett–Gherga–Kreso for length 3). States the finiteness of all solutions is unknown.
events.revisions: v1 19 Sep 2024; v2 3 Jan 2025 (the published version, one typo corrected); Integers 24 (2024) A98. The day of journal publication was not found.
events.delivers: For the restricted class where N is prime: no further solution with N < 10⁷⁰⁰ beyond N = 31 and N = 8191. Restrictions: N prime; N below 10⁷⁰⁰; computational. The conditional part holds only under abc: finitely many Goormaghtigh numbers where neither representation has length 3 or 4, and finitely many Goormaghtigh primes. The paper does not address composite N or prime N ≥ 10⁷⁰⁰.
events.remains: Composite N at every size; prime N at or above 10⁷⁰⁰; the unconditional finiteness question; every other part of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Satvik Beri and Joshua Zelinsky, 'On near superperfect numbers, the Goormaghtigh conjecture, and Mertens' theorem', arXiv:2505.08160 (v1 13 May 2025; v2 22 May 2025). The paper concerns Kalita–Saikia near superperfect numbers. On the Goormaghtigh side, it restates the conjecture as its Conjecture 7 with solutions (x, y, m, n) = (5, 2, 3, 5) and (90, 2, 3, 13) (letter order as in the statement's ordering), notes that the conjecture implies its Conjecture 8 (no odd Kalita–Saikia near superperfect numbers), and uses Yuan's result for n = 3 to tighten a near-superperfect theorem (Theorem 9). The abstract says only that the results are connected to the conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 13 May 2025; v2 22 May 2025 (current as of the arXiv page). No journal version found.
events.delivers: Nothing about the Goormaghtigh equation's solutions. It proves a conditional implication: if the conjecture holds, there are no odd Kalita–Saikia near superperfect numbers. It proves no new case of the equation and uses one known case as an input.
events.time_since_posted: about 17 months; no public engagement found
events.direction: Does not bear on whether further solutions exist; it assumes the conjecture for a conditional implication only.

events.what_happened: Tomohiro Yamada, 'On the Ratat–Goormaghtigh equation and integer points close to the graph of a smooth function', arXiv:2510.11252, v1 13 Oct 2025 (single version, 12 pp.). Studies (xᵐ − 1)/(x − 1) = N for a fixed N, bounding the sum of reciprocals of solutions x other than the smallest by 5.9037, and by 0.73194 when x is restricted to primes. The introduction states the Ratat and Goormaghtigh solutions, states the conjecture that the two solutions are the only solutions of the full equation with x, y ≥ 2 and m, n ≥ 3, and cites Bennett–Garbuz–Martens Lemma 2.3. Discounted for scope: its theorems concern fixed N only.
events.delivers: For a fixed N, bounds on reciprocal sums over solutions of (xᵐ − 1)/(x − 1) = N. Nothing proved about the full equation with both sides varying.
events.time_since_posted: about 12 months; no public engagement found
events.direction: Not about the conjecture's direction; a different (fixed-N) question. Its introduction restates the conjecture.

events.what_happened: A Hugging Face dataset repository, PureOne/goormaghtigh-equation-frontier-synthesis-v11, titled 'Goormaghtigh Equation Frontier Synthesis v11.0.0: Two-Chart Reconstruction, Radical Bounds, Exact Fibres, and Proof-Carrying Computation', release v11.0.0 dated 28 September 2026. The listed author is 'Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki'; the identity is not verified. The manuscript (MANUSCRIPT.md, opened) considers R_m(x) = R_n(y) with x > y ≥ 2 and 3 ≤ m < n, which is the statement's equation in its ordering. It claims an unconditional two-chart reduction: each solution maps to a primitive triple (Chart A: U + V = W; Theorem AT: A + B = C with C³⁶ > rad(ABC)³⁷), each fixed triple has a finite computable inverse fibre (Theorem F), and all solutions with height up to H are found by a finite enumeration (Theorem H; a normalised-height 10¹² enumeration is reported). It also gives exact results for adjacent lengths n = m + 1 (Theorem P, gcd(x, y) = 1, all m ≥ 3; Theorem 4, computer-assisted, 3 ≤ m ≤ 13). Its own PROOF_BOUNDARY.md and manuscript say the conjecture is not proved: no global height cutoff, no unconditional finite list of the triples, and the claim that no further inverse fibre is non-empty is not proved. The repository says the work is not peer reviewed or proof-assistant formalised.
events.revisions: The changelog lists one entry, v11.0.0 (28 Sep 2026). Provenance files refer to an earlier FLOQUET_TRANSFER_FROM_V7.md; versions v1–v10 are not dated or visible.
events.delivers: Claimed: (i) a reduction of every solution to a primitive abc-type triple, with radical quality C³⁶ > rad(ABC)³⁷ stated as unconditional; (ii) for each fixed triple, a finite decision procedure listing the solutions that map to it; (iii) for each height bound H, a finite enumeration of solutions up to H in Chart A; (iv) adjacent-length results for n = m + 1 with gcd(x, y) = 1 (all m ≥ 3, Theorem P) and computer-checked for 3 ≤ m ≤ 13 (Theorem 4). Conditional: assuming that for every δ > 0 only finitely many primitive triples satisfy C > rad(ABC)^(1+δ), the equation has finitely many solutions, though the document says this does not identify them as the two known solutions. None of this classifies the solutions; the two known solutions are not excluded by the code.
events.remains: The global step (no further non-empty inverse fibre beyond the two known solutions); a global height cutoff; an unconditional finite list of the relevant triples; the d = 1 branch and even-n quadratic cases (unbounded components); unbounded m and k. The adjacent-length results cover only n = m + 1 with gcd(x, y) = 1 for Theorem P.
events.directly_checkable: The repository ships Python 3.10+ standard-library code (verify_release.py, src/, tests/, certificates/), and the README says the declared computations are replayable from source. I did not download or run it. No Lean or Coq artefact is listed; the repository says it is not proof-assistant formalised.
events.doubts: (1) Self-published; the listed author's identity is unverified and a search for the name found nothing. (2) Self-declared not peer reviewed and not formalised. (3) The manuscript says 'global novelty is not established' and acknowledges prior work by Laishram–Shorey on the general normalisation and abc direction; its own status file says the unconditional radical-quality claim and the finiteness conclusion rely on standard abc. (4) Theorem 4 and the adjacent-length classifications are computer-assisted, with the code published by the same author. (5) Repository files addressed to AI research agents (AGENTS.md 'Research-agent rules', AI_CONTEXT.md, llms.txt) suggest agent-directed work, but no system is named (see ai).
events.direction: Partial reduction towards the conjecture; claims no new solution, does not claim the conjecture, and states that the two known solutions are not excluded by its code. Where it proves anything, it cuts toward finiteness and classification in the covered parts, with no counterexample reported.

ai.disclosed_cost: None disclosed. The README says there is 'no GPU hardware requirement'; the code needs Python 3.10 or newer and only the standard library. No compute time or token counts found. The manuscript states it 'does not execute a trained neural transformer'.

disputes.summary: Beri and Zelinsky attribute to Yuan the case n = 3 of the Goormaghtigh conjecture. The Wikipedia article, as summarised, attributes to Yuan (2005) the case m = 3 with n odd. These are different exponent conditions. Yuan's paper was not opened, so neither reading is confirmed.

The venue for Le's 2002 paper on x = 3 is reported inconsistently: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik in one search summary, and an Acta Mathematica Sinica listing with the same formula in another. The paper was not opened.

summary: The problem is open. I searched for the equation under its name and under the 'repunit in two bases' and 'Goormaghtigh primes' phrasings, for recent work in number theory, and for AI involvement, as DEEP_DIVE §4 requires. The main events since January 2024 are: (1) Grantham's arXiv preprint 'No new Goormaghtigh primes up to 10⁷⁰⁰' (v1 19 Sep 2024; Integers 24 (2024), A98), which finds no further prime N below 10⁷⁰⁰ with two repunit representations and proves, under abc, finiteness for a sub-case. This is a bounded search of the restricted prime class and, under the §2.1 scope test, may move no quantity the conjecture asks for, since it checks finitely many instances of a claim about all N. (2) Beri and Zelinsky (arXiv 13 May 2025) restate the conjecture and prove only a conditional implication about near-superperfect numbers; they do not move the problem. (3) Yamada (arXiv 13 Oct 2025) works on the fixed-N equation and is off-scope. (4) A Hugging Face repository, 'Goormaghtigh Equation Frontier Synthesis v11.0.0', released 28 Sep 2026, claims an unconditional reduction of solutions to abc-type triples, with finite inverse fibres per triple, height enumerations, and adjacent-length results for n = m + 1. The repository is self-published with a listed author whose identity I could not verify, and it says it is not peer reviewed or formalised. Its own PROOF_BOUNDARY.md and manuscript say the conjecture is not proved and list the missing global step. Pre-window literature, read through secondary summaries and the Grantham and Yamada reference lists, includes Davenport–Lewis–Schinzel (1961), Bateman–Stemmler (1962), Balasubramanian–Shorey (1980), Nesterenko–Shorey (1998), Yuan (2005), He–Togbé (2008), Bennett–Garbuz–Martens (manuscript Jan 2019; Publ. Math. Debrecen 2020), Bennett–Gherga–Kreso (TAMS 2020), and Fujita–Le (online 23 June 2023, which settles the base shape (pʳ, pˢ+1) with one solution (2,5,5,3)). AI: no source names an AI system involved in the mathematics. The Hugging Face repository has agent-orientation files (AGENTS.md 'Research-agent rules', AI_CONTEXT.md, llms.txt) and says its code does not run a trained neural model, but it names no model and does not say how the text was written, so AI involvement is neither named nor excluded for that work. Close calls: whether Grantham's prime-only computation counts as moving any quantity the conjecture asks for (it is one finite instance check of a restricted class); whether the 2026 manuscript's reduction is a classification step or a reformulation. Discrepancies I could not resolve: the attribution of Yuan's result (n = 3 versus m = 3 with n odd) and the venue of Le 2002. Grantham's 10⁷⁰⁰ search and the 2026 manuscript's computations are not independently rerun. The 2026 HF listed author ('Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki') appears nowhere else in the search results and is not a name I could identify with a person or a system.
competing_reading: Grantham's search settles every prime N below 10⁷⁰⁰ and could be read as a real advance on the classification, since primes are the natural hard case. On the §2.1 test it is one more finite instance of a universal claim, so it moves nothing the conjecture asks for. The 2026 HF manuscript could be read as a genuine partial classification: its Chart A and Theorem AT reduce every solution to finitely many candidate triples per height, and its adjacent-length results are exact. Against that reading, the manuscript says the reduction is 'not its resolution', states the missing global step, and has no peer review or formalisation, and its author cannot be identified. Its AI status is also unclear: agent-facing files and a 'research-agent rules' document are present, but no system is named.
what_would_settle_it: For the 2026 manuscript: an independent check of Theorem AT's inequality (C³⁶ > rad(ABC)³⁷), the Theorem F decision procedure, and the missing global step, by a number theorist or a Lean formalisation, plus an identifiable author and a statement of how the text and code were produced. For Grantham: a published rerun or extension of the 10⁷⁰⁰ search, and the typeset Theorem 2 to check the length 3–4 versus m < 5 point. For the classification: a proof that the union of inverse fibres over the high-quality triples is exactly the two known solutions, or a further solution. For Yuan 2005 and Le 2002: the primary papers, to settle the exponent attribution and the venue.
